newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese businessmen fear policy change.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese businessmen fear policy change.

text.p: Lebanese businessmen expressed concern on Monday that drastic changes in import policies ordered by the government last week could signal the start of a move away from economic liberalism.

The Lebanese Business Managers Grouping (LBMG) called the decisions to raise duties on luxury cars by up to 200 percent and to ban import of those foods already grown in Lebanon improvised, ill-considered and hasty.

The group, a private association based in Beirut which says it represents 300 businessmen across Lebanon, said the government had acted without studying the consequences of its actions or consulting concerned parties.
Both the decisions and the way they were taken caused concern that Lebanon could face further unpredictable policy turns in the future, it said.

"How can one not expect other 'surprises' that could cause caution among investors who rely on the continuation of a certain economic path?" the group said in a half-page statement in Beirut newspapers.
"The grouping...fears that the repetition of such decisions might hit the bases of liberal trends," it said.

"The grouping stresses the importance of setting principles and rules...while the basics of the Lebanese economy remain clear and possible changes are limited to a certain framework, namely the preservation of a liberal economy and openness to the outside," the statement said.

Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri has denied that the measures signal a move away from economic liberalism or an adjustment of the economy to the state-controlled socialist policies of Lebanon's powerful neighbour Syria.

"Our economy is free and will remain so. These measures are not the prelude to changing our economic system, nor to economic complementarity with Syria, as some people think," Hariri was quoted as saying last week.

This has not stopped speculation in the Beirut press that the decisions indicate that the Lebanese economy could be brought under Syria's sway in the same way that its politics have increasingly fallen under Syrian hegemony in recent years.
In economic terms the new car duties and the food import restrictions will help reduce Lebanon's massive trade deficit which totalled $6.5 billion last year.

The government said too many cars were being imported for a country of Lebanon's size and the food restrictions would slash a $1.5 billion annual food import bill by 20 percent initially when they take effect in October.
This would give Lebanese agriculture a chance to develop, Agriculture Minister Chawki Fakhoury said.

However, half a dozen other ministers have denounced the decisions and Economy Minister Yassine Jaber said ministers only saw the proposals 15 minutes before the cabinet meeting. He would not let his ministry monitor food imports and prices.
Agriculture experts have said the food import restrictions could not themselves improve production but could cause smuggling, increase the price of domestic products and cause a fall in quality.

The businessmen said the decisions had inserted an element of ambiguity into Lebanon's economic policy: "How can we pretend openness while we establish protectionism, seek competition while opening the door to monopoly?...How can we improve quality without competing with foreign production?" they said.
